title: Broken Ergodicity and the Violation of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem Lead to Generalization Beyond Overfitting in Machine Learning
abstract: The remarkable ability of modern neural networks to generalize improves with increasing network capacity, even when the number of model parameters or effective degrees of freedom exceeds the number of training data points. This phenomenon is all the more surprising given that generalization error diverges when the number of model parameters approaches a critical value from below. Here we use dynamical mean field theory to show that this so-called "double descent" behavior is the outcome of a phase transition in the stochastic field theory describing the training process. We calculate the critical exponents and scaling function of the double descent phase transition, and show that it is marked by a breakdown of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem associated with broken ergodicity. The corresponding response function has the same functional form as the simple London model of the superconducting transition, with the rigidity of the wave function corresponding to the neural network's ability to generalize accurately.
summary: This theoretical work explains 'double descent' by modeling neural network training as a dynamical phase transition. It shows that the improved generalization in overparameterized regimes is mathematically equivalent to breaking ergodicity, mirroring physics seen in superconductors where the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem breaks down.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a theoretical explanation for the 'double descent' phenomenon in overparameterized neural networks, where generalization error decreases again beyond the interpolation threshold.
main_result: This double descent behavior is shown to be the outcome of a dynamical phase transition characterized by the breakdown of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (FDT) and broken ergodicity.
method: The analysis employs Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) applied to the stochastic gradient flow describing the training process, comparing it to known critical phenomena in condensed matter physics.
model_or_system: The system models the training dynamics of a linear student network learning from a teacher model. The mathematical framework involves analyzing correlation and response functions derived from the SGD process in the thermodynamic limit.
key_observables: Generalization error ($\epsilon_g$), training error ($\epsilon_t$), Response function ($R(t, t')$), Correlation function ($C(t, t')$), and the violation of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (FDT).
important_parameters: The overparameterization ratio $\alpha = d/N$, which dictates the system's regime ($\alpha < 1$ vs. $\alpha > 1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the learning dynamics onto established models from statistical physics, particularly drawing analogies to superconducting transitions and normal metals.
figures_summary: Figures likely compare the scaling of generalization error ($\epsilon_g$) across different regimes ($\alpha$), showing a transition point analogous to $T_c$ or $\alpha=1$, and illustrating the functional form of the response function in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the ML problem (double descent), then mapping it onto a physical model using DMFT, analyzing the critical behavior at the interpolation threshold ($\alpha=1$), and finally interpreting the resulting FDT violation as the mechanism for generalization in the overparameterized regime.
why_interesting: The direct analogy drawn between superconducting phase transitions (a hallmark of non-equilibrium dynamics) and benign overfitting provides a powerful, physical framework for understanding modern deep learning phenomena.
